texto:
An average minute rating (AMR) is the audience of a programme, time slot, commercial break or advertisement, calculated by counting the viewers present in every minute it ran and then averaging those counts. Expressed as a percentage of a defined population, it is a rating; expressed as a number of people, it is usually called the average minute audience (AMA). The measure exists because a television audience is never fixed. People arrive late, leave at half-time and switch channels during breaks, so a single headcount at any one moment misstates who watched. Averaging across every minute gives one comparable figure for content of any length, and that figure is what broadcasters publish, agencies plan against and advertisers pay for.
How the average is built
The calculation starts with a measurement panel. In the United States, Nielsen's national service combines about 101,000 people in 42,000 panel homes with device tuning data from roughly 45 million households, a system called Big Data + Panel that replaced panel-only ratings for the 2025 season, as PPC Land reported when Nielsen ended its legacy ratings. In the United Kingdom, Barb uses a panel of 7,000 homes run by Kantar Media. Italy's Auditel, Turkey's TIAK and other national bodies run comparable panels.
Each panel member's viewing is first resolved into clock minutes. Barb's rule illustrates the mechanics. A person counts in the audience for a minute if present in the room with the set on for at least 31 seconds of that clock minute, and the minute is attributed to the channel the set was tuned to longest within it, according to the Barb glossary published by Thinkbox. Panel members are then weighted so that the sample represents the whole population, and each minute receives an estimated audience.
The average follows. Auditel defines AMR as "the average of the number of viewers for each one of the single minutes included in a programme or time slot," according to its glossary. A worked example shows the arithmetic. A 60-minute programme in a market of 10 million people draws 2 million viewers per minute for its first half and 1 million for its second. The average minute audience is 1.5 million. Divided by the 10 million universe, the rating is 15.
Three related figures come from the same minute data. Share divides the programme's audience by everyone watching television at the time, so if 5 million people were watching anything on average, the programme's share is 30 per cent. Gross rating points (GRPs) add up the ratings of every spot in a campaign. Commercial ratings apply the average to advertising minutes rather than programme minutes. The Coalition for Innovative Media Measurement notes that an average audience rating "can be parsed to the lowest viewing increment whether second, 5 second, minute etc."
Terminology varies by country, and this causes confusion. Auditel uses AMR for the number of viewers and TVR for the percentage. Nielsen speaks of average audience and AMA. Barb calls the percentage a TVR and the count a programme average audience. The underlying calculation is the same in each case.
Where it sits in the market
Measurement companies produce the figure, but buyers and sellers decide which version counts. On the sell side, networks report programme AMAs to the press and sell advertising against them. On the buy side, agencies plan reach and frequency from ratings and verify delivery afterwards. In the US upfront market, deals carry an audience guarantee usually stated in GRPs, and a seller that falls short delivers extra inventory later, a mechanism set out in PPC Land's upfront explainer.
The rating that settles those deals is not the programme average. C3, the average commercial minute rating, counts the audience for the average minute containing advertising, adding three days of playback to live viewing. It has anchored US upfront deals since 2007, as PPC Land's currency explainer describes. Which days of playback are included is a separate question about time-shifted viewing. The averaging method itself stays the same.
From quarter hours to minutes
Early ratings were coarse. Paper diaries, which Nielsen began using in 1953, recorded viewing in quarter-hour blocks. The average quarter-hour (AQH) became the standard unit, and it survives in radio and local television.
Electronic people meters brought minute-level data. Barb's Enhanced Measurement System became operational in December 1984, when "the people meter replaces the set meter and paper diaries," according to Barb's history pages. Nielsen formally launched its national people meter service on August 31, 1987, according to John Dimling, a former Nielsen Media Research chief executive, quoted by RBR.
The commercial version followed two decades later. Nielsen launched commercial ratings on May 31, 2007, according to WARC. The first week of data arrived about two weeks after the upfront presentations. Shari Anne Brill of Carat USA explained to RBR at the time that any programme minute containing at least one second of national advertising was flagged as a commercial minute, and Nielsen produced a weighted average of those minutes. She called it a gauge of potential audience for an ad message rather than a true ad rating. Sources disagree on what began in 2007. Wikipedia's entry states that Nielsen introduced AMA that year, but minute-level averages existed in people-meter data long before; 2007 is better understood as the year the average commercial minute became a currency.
Streaming forced the next change. Nielsen's Big Data + Panel launched on September 2, 2025, and the Super Bowl in February 2026 was the first reported on that basis. On August 31, 2026, Nielsen applied seven methodology changes, including wearable devices that capture co-viewing, as PPC Land reported on the seven currency changes.
Why the number carries weight
AMA is the figure that headlines record. Super Bowl LX on February 8, 2026, averaged 125.6 million viewers across NBC, Peacock, Telemundo and digital platforms, according to Nielsen. That was second only to Super Bowl LIX's 127.7 million in February 2025. The 2026 total had initially been reported as 124.9 million and was revised upward after a big data provider failed to collect device data on the day, according to Nielsen.
Streaming services adopted the same unit when they began selling live sport. Netflix's Christmas Day NFL games in December 2024 averaged 24.3 million and 24.1 million US viewers, AMA figures based on Nielsen Fast National Live + Same Day data combined with Netflix's own mobile and web data, according to Streaming Media Blog. YouTube's first exclusive NFL game, played in Sao Paulo on September 5, 2025, was reported at 17.3 million global AMA, according to YouTube. Using one unit allows a streamer to place its audience beside a broadcast network's in front of advertisers who price both.
Where it is contested
The average hides shape. A three-hour awards show that loses half its audience can post a lower AMR than a 30-minute sitcom with fewer total viewers. Networks often counter with peak figures. NBC promoted Super Bowl LX's peak of 137.8 million, recorded between 7:45 and 8:00 pm ET, 12.2 million more than the average, according to Nielsen.
Company-reported AMAs are hard to audit. Netflix said its November 2024 boxing match between Jake Paul and Mike Tyson drew 108 million global viewers, according to MediaPost, which noted the company did not explain how the figure was calculated. YouTube revised its Brazil NFL game from 17.3 million to 19.7 million AMA on September 12, 2025, after a technical issue caused some legitimate views not to be counted, according to its own correction. Outside the US, that audience came from YouTube's internal data, not an independent panel.
Crediting rules also differ. A minute in Barb requires 31 seconds of presence. Digital video standards count far shorter exposures, which makes cross-platform comparisons uneven. Who counts as present is unsettled too. Nielsen's co-viewing pilot, using wearables, raised total viewers by an average of 4.19 per cent across seven live events in February 2026, according to a Nielsen release on May 5, 2026. Those numbers were excluded from currency. Measurement access is a further dispute: Barb paused its reporting of YouTube channels after Google sent cease-and-desist letters, as PPC Land reported in January 2026.
Not the same as
Reach. Reach counts distinct people who saw at least some of the content. Nielsen put Super Bowl LIX's reach, defined as viewers who watched at least one minute, at 171.8 million after a revision on February 5, 2026, against an average of 127.7 million. Barb requires three consecutive minutes.
Share. Share uses only people watching television as its denominator. A programme can gain share while its rating falls, if total viewing falls faster.
Peak or concurrent viewers. A peak is the single highest minute or quarter hour. Streaming services report peak concurrent streams, which count devices, not people.
Average quarter-hour rating. AQH averages 15-minute blocks and credits a viewer only after a qualifying period. Nielsen cut that local TV qualifier from five minutes to one on August 31, 2026, as PPC Land reported.
Recent developments
The minute-level average is being rebuilt from new inputs rather than replaced. Nielsen's August 31, 2026, changes put wearable co-viewing data and adjusted universe estimates into the national service, and Nielsen said there was "no guarantee of increased ratings as a result." It aims to bring wearable co-viewing into currency for the 2026-27 season, subject to validation, as PPC Land reported on the Super Bowl pilot. The metric has also spread beyond television. On October 15, 2026, Riot Games reported a 714,000 AMA for the 2026 season of the LCK, South Korea's top League of Legends league, the first time it passed 700,000, according to the Seoul Economic Daily.
Timeline
- 1953 - Nielsen begins collecting TV viewing through paper diaries, recorded in quarter hours.
- 1981 - Barb is established as the UK's TV audience measurement body.
- December 1984 - Barb's Enhanced Measurement System goes live and people meters replace set meters and diaries.
- August 31, 1987 - Nielsen formally launches its national people meter service.
- May 31, 2007 - Nielsen launches commercial ratings; C3 becomes the currency for the 2007-08 season.
- November 2024 - Netflix reports 108 million global viewers for Paul vs Tyson without disclosing method.
- December 25, 2024 - Netflix's NFL Christmas games average 24.3 million and 24.1 million US viewers.
- January 24, 2025 - Nielsen announces the end of panel-only national ratings.
- February 9, 2025 - Super Bowl LIX averages a record 127.7 million viewers.
- September 2, 2025 - Nielsen Big Data + Panel launches for the 2025 season.
- September 5, 2025 - YouTube's Brazil NFL game is reported at 17.3 million global AMA, later revised to 19.7 million.
- January 28, 2026 - Barb confirms its YouTube channel measurement service is paused.
- February 8, 2026 - Super Bowl LX averages 125.6 million, the first Super Bowl reported on Big Data + Panel.
- May 5, 2026 - Nielsen reports a 4.19 per cent average co-viewing uplift from its wearables pilot.
- August 31, 2026 - Nielsen applies seven national currency changes and a one-minute local tuning qualifier.
- October 15, 2026 - Riot Games reports a 714,000 AMA for the 2026 LCK season.

Summary
Who. Measurement companies such as Nielsen in the US, Barb with Kantar Media in the UK and Auditel in Italy produce the figure. Networks and streaming services report it, agencies plan against it and advertisers buy on it.
What. The average number of viewers, or percentage of a population, watching across every minute of a programme, slot, break or ad. As a count it is the average minute audience; as a percentage it is a rating or TVR.
When. Minute-level averages arrived with people meters in 1984 in the UK and 1987 in the US. The average commercial minute became US currency in 2007, and Nielsen's Big Data + Panel replaced panel-only inputs in September 2025.
Where. Every major national TV market, now extended to streaming live events and esports. Rules on crediting a minute differ by country and platform.
Why. Audiences change minute to minute. A per-minute average gives one comparable number for content of any length, which is why it anchors ratings headlines, audience guarantees and the price of TV advertising.
